newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Oil prices tiptoe higher but doubts remain.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Oil prices tiptoe higher but doubts remain.

text.p: World oil prices inched higher on Monday as the market took stock of a rally at the end of last week and awaited fresh news to confirm the trend.
Friday's rally lifted prices off a 13-month low set last week after a slide lasting nearly a month, and left dealers wondering which way the market would move next.
"The question now facing the oil market is whether or not this recent price fall is likely to continue in the coming months," the Centre for Global Energy Studies (CGES) said in a report.

August futures for Benchmark Brent Blend crude finished trading in London at $17.86 a barrel, 10 cents up on the day, while in New York the front-month WTI contract ended 13 cents up at $18.96 a barrel.

Some brokers said continuing delays to the second six-month tranche of Iraqi exports covered by a humanitarian agreement between the United Nations and Iraq would heighten short-term supply worries and buoy prices.
Iraqi envoy Nizar Hamdoon said last week no more oil would be exported until Baghdad received assurances on the distribution of food and medicine bought with the proceeds of its crude exports.
U.N. diplomats told Reuters Iraq would probably be allowed to pump the full $2 billion of oil in a shortened four- or five-month period if its exports were delayed.
The original terms of the oil-for-food deal called for $1 billion worth of sales each 90 days.
With U.N. sources saying Iraq is unlikely to complete work on the food distribution plan until the end of June, brokers said the saga could lift prices.
"Iraq is providing a fundamental push for higher prices," said broker GNI.

But there was also a possibility that a delay in the Iraq deal could prompt a medium-term supply glut which could be enhanced if OPEC countries meeting in Vienna next Wednesday fail to agree on stringent adherence to production quotas.
While a handful of Gulf producers led by Saudi Arabia are maintaining spare capacity and quota discipline, others like Venezuela and Nigeria are pumping at full steam without regard for oil prices.
Analysts saw little chance of a change in approach and warned that rising output from producers outside the 11-member cartel could spell lower prices later in the year.
"Once again, it is non-OPEC output that is providing the major uncertainty on the supply side," the GCES said.
Further evidence of oversupply was seen in Asia, where Shell Singapore said on Monday poor profit margins had forced it to cut refining output.
However, industry sources said the move was unlikely to have any real impact on prices or profits.
"It is a drop in the bucket when you look at the regional refining capacity. The storage tanks in Singapore look quite full and there isn't much demand out there," said a refinery source.
